query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 1–2 wt% Ni into a W–Cu composite via ball-milling and subsequent high-temperature sintering/infiltration will reduce interfacial defects (phase separation and voids) and improve thermal conductivity under fusion-relevant heat flux and irradiation conditions compared to the same W–Cu composite without Ni doping.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
generation.intervention: Low-level Ni doping (1–2 wt%) introduced by ball-milling a W–Cu + Ni powder blend, followed by a high-temperature densification step (e.g., sintering or infiltration).
generation.conditions: Typical operating conditions for tungsten-based plasma-facing materials joined to copper-based heat sinks: heat loads of ~10–20 MW/m2 and concurrent neutron/ion irradiation in fusion-relevant environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Ni atoms segregated at the W–Cu interface, stabilizing the interface and inhibiting deleterious interfacial reactions.
generation.mechanism: Nickel doping lowers interfacial energy, limiting void nucleation and suppressing excessive W–Cu phase separation under extreme heat flux and irradiation. This preserves continuous thermal conduction pathways and reduces interface degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped W–Cu composite, the Ni-doped material will exhibit reduced interfacial porosity and higher retained thermal conductivity in service.
generation.baseline: Performance of an equivalent W–Cu composite without any Ni addition, processed under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Doping levels above ~2 wt% Ni may introduce secondary phases or degrade thermal properties; applicability is limited to W–Cu-based heat-sink and plasma-facing applications exposed to high heat fluxes and moderate neutron/ion irradiation.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Ni content and processing window remain to be fully validated for long-duration irradiation in real reactor environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu samples with identical tungsten volume fraction: one set doped with 1–2 wt% Ni, and one undoped. Subject both sets to identical high heat flux and ion/neutron irradiation exposure representative of reactor wall conditions.
measurements: Microstructural inspection via electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to quantify interfacial voids and elemental segregation.
Steady-state thermal conductivity measurements before and after irradiation.
Mechanical integrity (tensile or bend tests) to assess any irradiation-induced embrittlement.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under these conditions, the Ni-doped composite exhibits similar or worse interfacial integrity or thermal conductivity degradation compared to undoped W–Cu, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. chosen.lever: Nickel doping (1–2 wt%) into W–Cu composite
chosen.technique: Ball-milling of W–Cu+Ni powders followed by sintering/infiltration
chosen.conditions: Elevated-temperature and irradiation conditions matching plasma-facing joints
chosen.why: Nickel doping at the W–Cu interface is a straightforward, well-established approach to reduce phase separation and inhibit void formation under high heat flux and irradiation.
